utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marusic. Please be so kind as to give the Honourable Judges your exact name and surname.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I'm Ivo Marusic. I was born on the 17th of September, 1965, in the village of Jasvine, municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm going to lead you as far as your C.V. is concerned so we'll get through that quickly. You completed elementary school in Busovaca, and your secondary education, the Mining and Geological School, in Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After finishing secondary school in 1984, you did your compulsory military service in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Upon completing your military service, you enrolled at the mechanical engineering faculty in Zenica. However, due to the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991, or rather 1992, and your wish to take part in the defence of your homeland, you interrupted your studies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After the end of the war in 1994, you continued your studies at the university of Mostar, where you graduated in 1995. You are a mechanical engineer by profession.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1993 to May 1994, you were a member of the 1st Company or the 1st Battalion of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Busovaca. However, you hold no military rank; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On the 16th of March, 1996, you began to work as the head of the defence office in Busovaca. You worked there until the 1st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On the 1st of March, 1999, you were transferred to the police administration in Busovaca, where you work until the present day, and you are now head of the Busovaca police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, I would now like to draw your attention to the following. Actually, for the reasons why you are here in this Court today. As you were head of the defence office in Busovaca, one of your duties was to submit proposals for awarding decorations to persons who had given a certain contribution during the war to the defence against the Serb, that is, Muslim aggression during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You submitted these proposals for persons who were employed in your office, who were employed then, that is, or who were employed earlier?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please: These persons for whom you submitted proposals in October, were they only civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: They were exclusively civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: While you were submitting this request, you did not have enough personal knowledge as to who were all the persons who worked in that office before, because, as we said a few minutes ago, you were rank-and-file soldier during the war, so I imagine that you asked around, you consulted people in the municipality of Busovaca about who these persons who worked in this office before you came there were.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: That's right. I just started working in the office after the war, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. The interpreters can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I imagine you talked to the head of the municipality at that time, Mr. Nikola Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, we're getting a request that the witness speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you speak up a bit, Mr. Marusic, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can I request that the evidence be not led at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you understand this question, or should I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood you. I started working in the defence office in 1996, in March, that is to say, the end of the war. Since I was a soldier, I had not worked in these institutions. That is to say that I was not familiar with who held which post and who were all the persons who worked in the defence office from 1991 until the end of the war. So at one of the meetings that was held with the head of the municipality at that time, Nikola Grubesic, and also the former head of the office, Mr. Katava, I had a conversation as to who were all the people who passed through this office, who worked in this office, and who had certain merits for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You acted upon instructions, the instructions that you got from the office in Travnik, and according to these instructions, you were supposed to submit the names of persons who are either employed in the Busovaca defence office or who worked there earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had instructions from the administration of defence in Travnik; that is to say, at the level of this administration, eight decorations could have been proposed for ten offices all together; that is to say, that these decorations were to be bestowed only upon persons who worked in these defence offices as civilians, who worked there earlier or who were still employed there; that is, so I proposed, after these consultations were held and all the rest, I decided to propose two men for these decorations. So in October 1996, I proposed Mr. Vinko Markovic who was an official of the office then and still is, as well as Mr. Kordic who worked as head of the office from 1991 until the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, you personally signed this proposal both for Mr. Kordic and for Mr. Markovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I signed this proposal. I mean I wrote the text of this proposal and Mr. Markovic, who is an employee at the office anyway, and who was in charge of typing this up did so. So when he completed the typing, I decided to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you made a draft of this text. When Mr. Markovic typed it out, you approved it, so to speak, and you signed it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D1477. I'm sorry, Z1477, there's been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The front page has been put on the ELMO. Tell me, please, this front page that we see on the ELMO now, that is the proposal that you signed and that you sent to the administration of defence in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: This is the accompanying letter with the proposal that was sent. This is a form. This page is an accompanying document along with the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So the proposal that you made was actually this form. You filled out this form that you had received, and this is how proposals were submitted?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a form and that is what we got along with the request for the submission of proposals. This proposal is called D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Marusic, please, when drafting these proposals both for Mr. Markovic and for Mr. Kordic, what kind of words did you use? What kind of words did you use when you made these proposals, and what is customary, generally speaking, when such proposals are being drafted?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, before, in the administration for defence in Travnik, we had a meeting, consultations with regard to filling out these forms. It was customary for these proposals to be filled out quite carefully and they were supposed to be spruced up, so to speak. We were supposed to pay attention to every word, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand what you're saying, your instructions were to do this through chosen words; is that what you are trying to say and is that customary?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Every decoration had --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, we'll go back to that later. Now we're talking about the form. You have before you the proposal for Mr. Kordic, and there is a text here under item 15. The text that you wrote or rather signed. Tell me, please, to the best of your knowledge, was Mr. Kordic a military person or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, he was not a military person. He was a civilian person. He was an official in the office of defence during that period of time, and that is a civilian institution an exclusively civilian institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you personally, you are familiar with the contribution that Mr. Kordic gave at that time precisely while he was an official in the defence office in Busovaca in 1991 and somewhat later?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I personally know about this. He played a significant role on several occasions together with other citizens. He went out into the streets to block the passage of convoys of the former JNA that were coming to the territory of Busovaca and they wished to go further. He gave quite a contribution because at that time he was head of the defence office. His significant contribution lay in the fact that together with the then head of the TO headquarters, Mr. Hadzimejlic, he deferred the departure of conscripts to the former JNA which resounded rather favourably. That would have meant that we would have fought against ourselves, that we would be killing ourselves through the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, you were a member of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade for over a year, that is to say, in 1993 and part of 1994. Did you ever hear of Mr. Kordic having issued an order to the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade or any other military unit?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I never heard of Mr. Kordic having issued any kind of order. We received our orders exclusively through the command, the headquarters of the 1st Battalion and the 1st Battalion from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, in the document you have submitted to us, and which we can no longer see, maybe it might be useful to put it on the ELMO, I'd like to ask this of the witness. He says that Mr. Kordic had no military role whatsoever, that he only had a civilian role. How does he understand the following sentence if he indeed signed this document, where it is stated that [In English] "Of all of the Croats in central Bosnia, he played a key role in all the battles." [In French] Can a civilian play a key role, a central role in all battles? Now, how does the witness understand that sentence?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, this sentence, at the end of the text, as far as I understood it, that is to say, this was a turning point in all the battles. At quite a few times, it was rather difficult at the front line, quite a few people lost their lives. We were encircled, and day after day, we were in a situation that we could not be replaced by anyone. There was no one to replace us. When we would get home, we did not even have sufficient morale. When I personally, for instance, when I would come home, I would be so tired and I really didn't have much morale. My parents told me that they heard from Mr. Kordic that he was addressing the people and that he said that we were the ones who had to remain in that area. So he, amongst the civilians, constituted this turning point. He was one of the persons who made it possible for us to fight so hard at the front line, and to be entrenched there. So in spite of being outnumbered, we could not be chased out of this area by anyone. This was a key thing with regard to our survival and to the war in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've failed to answer my question. You didn't quite answer it. You say he played a key role in all the battles. Does that mean that he had authority in the way the battles were conducted?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: He did not have authority. I emphasise that. He was a turning point in the struggle. That is to say, when we were on the ground, when we were engaged in battle, when there were crises, sometimes some people would even run away from the front line in order to get their families out of the area, to try to get out somehow. The families at home would hear, through the mass media at that time, these messages that were being sent out. So he only sent these messages to civilians, not to the military. On the one hand, we received orders at the front line from the military, from the headquarters, whereas civilians were receiving such messages from Mr. Kordic. He was addressing himself to all the expellees. He was going to see them in all the places they were staying, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can proceed straight away after this question put by the Honourable Judge Bennouna. So by way of a metaphor you explained this moral support that was given by Mr. Kordic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, let the witness give the evidence about this. It's obviously an important issue. Let him explain what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having cautioned me, Your Honour. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, this turning point, this meant hope and faith in our survival. This was an address to the population. These were messages that were being sent to us that in spite of all these horrors and in spite of the large numbers of the enemy, we had a chance of staying. So the messages that were being conveyed were these messages of boosting morale, that we could stay on if we were united.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please: We said already that this proposal was made on a form, by way of a form, OD-1. Please look at item 15 in this form, especially this instruction that is given in very fine print at the end of item 15 in the Croat text. Could you please read these instructions. How was this supposed to be written? Please read these instructions at the end of column 15.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: "Due to the unique historic importance of the decoration, take particular care when preparing this text. Do not use abbreviations in the text. Should the award be approved, the recommended text will be recorded in the award certificate."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please: The instructions here under item 15, what kind of an effect did this have on you? What conclusion did you draw on this basis? What were you supposed to write out in the proposal, and how were you supposed to write out this proposal? In which way?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I composed this proposal a few times. I redrafted it. Whenever I would write it out, it did not seem sufficient to me. It seemed to me that I had to spruce it up. There was an additional responsibility involved in terms of this decoration, because if the decoration were to be awarded, these words, this text, would be written out during the conferral of the decoration itself. So I tried to choose each and every word so that it would carry a certain weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So after you did what you say you did, and improved that text in line with these instructions, you signed the text, as you just told us?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I signed it personally and sent it to the defence administration in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please: In the introductory part of the document, under the item 8, part 1, particulars, 3, it says "rank" and it says "brigadier." Will you tell us, please: Once the information about the rank -- and what kind of a rank is it, to your knowledge, and when was it conferred upon?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: So this information comes from our records, from the card, from the personal card, and this is a rank of reserve officers conferred upon persons who were not active-duty army members but were nevertheless awarded the rank. We have such ranks. Every -- well, now every politician in Busovaca had such a rank of various military services, from infantry to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please: The Court has already heard testimony of [indiscernible] from Busovaca, Mr. Grubesic, Zoran Maric. They are all civilians. I do not think that is in question.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And that they shared political duties for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So tell us, please: To your knowledge, do they also have some reserve ranks?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do. I've just said so. Practically all the politicians were awarded these ranks, and I personally know, for instance, about Zoran Maric and Niko Grubesic, that they had some ranks too, even if somewhat lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So these honorary ranks were conferred upon them for their political work during the war, for the civilian duties they discharged?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we should like to adduce only one exhibit, and we shall be over soon. This will be the final subject we wish to raise. Mr. Usher, will you please help me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D283/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, will you tell us, please: To your knowledge, did Mr. Kordic and Mr. Markovic, pursuant to this proposal, ever conferred upon these decorations for which they were nominated [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, none of them received the decorations, because had they received them, I would have known, because they were sent to the office. And as I already said, we had those official ceremonies of the award of decorations, which means they did not get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you please look at this. This is a letter from the State Commission for Military Decorations of the Republic of Croatia. And it says that not only did Mr. Kordic never receive the decoration, but that this proposal was never filed with them. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Marusic, thank you Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the last document, of course, which would typically have been a matter of live evidence or affidavit evidence, I didn't object to it, although I can see the point that was arising evidentially from it. I'm not in any position to deal with it, and I don't accept it. There's nothing I can do about it. It's a way of getting evidence in just by a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marusic, His Honour Judge Bennouna asked you some questions, but before that you had signed a not very long summary of your evidence. Do you remember signing that summary apparently on the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you signed that summary, were you satisfied that everything in it was accurate and complete?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the particular question of His Honour Judge Bennouna didn't lead to you think that anything you had said might have been inaccurate or incomplete in the summary, didn't trigger some further recollection of how it was you had made this recommendation for an award?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you were asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a difficult point. The question by the Learned Judge didn't lead you suddenly to think, "Oh, dear, I've forgot about something and I should have put it in my statement."

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have anything else to add to my statement. That was the summary of the statement. Yeah, I am here to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me just eliminate a couple of points. You're not here to talk about Busovaca generally or about your time in the army, and I'm not going to ask, without leave, any questions about those matters. But just tell me, please, your service as a private in the 1st Battalion of the brigade from the beginning of 1993 and until May 1994 took you to which areas in general? Where were you involved in fighting?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Only on the front near my place of residence; that is, Roske Stijene, Bare, towards Rovna, that was the front line, and I was often assigned to stand guard by -- at Roske Stijene by the water supply system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were essentially operating only on a very local basis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to ask you any matters of detail about that. Between May 1994 and the time when you took up the job at the defence office, you were back at your studies, I think, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you took up the job in the defence office, what, immediately on graduating?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Not quite. I graduated in 1995 and I worked as a trainee for the Vitezit company in Vitez until March and then I moved over to the defence office. So between September 1995 and -- I worked for Vitezit until I joined the office department, I worked for the Vitezit company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The head of the defence office might sound to be a quite senior position for a fresh graduate, on the other hand, it may be a very small office so that there are only one or two people there. Is the head of the defence office quite a senior post?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people in the office at that time in 1996, just so that we have the picture?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is relatively high. There were 14 people there and I assumed the duty -- I mean after the war in those territories, practically all the young people who had come out of school, a larger number had gone abroad and, in a way, I came as a trainee without any noteworthy experience, except that I had graduated from university because, of course, there were certain terms for that job that one had to have the university degree. And had I come out of mechanical engineering, so I wasn't really qualified, because they were asking for a degree in humanities, but since those other people were in short supply, were not available, so I simply took up that office. I moved from the company that I had worked for to that particular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, did you have any connections, were you a member of the party, anything like that, just so that we have the picture complete in order to get that job?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was in Mostar, that is, I had not even gone back home yet, others were asking whether I would be coming or not so as to nominate me. And I've just told you there were very few qualified people in the area so that it wasn't all that difficult to get the job like that. And I started working in my profession as a professional, but in Vitezit, my salary was 300 German marks and over there, it was twice as high. So that I decided to change, and I was a supporter of that party and that was, at the time, the only party among the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You tell us that your inquiries were made to various people. Can you just name the people to whom you addressed questions before preparing this recommendation for an award? Who did you ask, in particular?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I said so, there were meetings of the municipal government in the municipal hall, and Jedinko Katava, who held that post before me, still works for the municipal government, but he is with the office of economy so that he was also at the meeting, and I talked to him and also to Mr. Gavro Maric who, at that time, discharged the duty of the head after Mr. Dario Kordic and now is with the defence administration in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Gavro Maric, was it? Is that the person you asked?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Gavro Maric works at the defence administration in Travnik and I was at a meeting there too when we talked about how the form had to be filled. He, for a while, headed the office after Mr. Kordic and then he moved over to the administration -- the defence administration and now works there and we received this from the defence administration, this thing to nominate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then you spoke to one of the Grubesics?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then you spoke to one of the Grubesics, who was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Niko Grubesic. Well, he was the head of the municipality and he was also at that meeting and Jedinko Katava, the former one, so there was at the same time conversation with Mr. Katava and Mr. Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are the important people you were speaking to, was there any other important person that you spoke to about these matters?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that was enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due apologies, I do not want to interfere, but just this moment, I've spotted a mistake between the English and Serbo-Croatian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, if it's on the text, I won't interrupt, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the name, it's the name. In paragraph six, and the witness said today he was talking to the then municipal mayor, Niko Grubesic, and in the English text it says Zoran Maric. That is the difference. I do apologise, but this is indeed, a slip and I've just spotted it. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I see, please, the original version of this witness' summary in Serbo-Croat, in Croatian? Can I see it, please? If it's really wrong, I will, of course, accept it. I'll come back to that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Niko Grubesic, to whom you say you spoke, would no doubt have a recollection of this important inquiry about granting an award to Mr. Kordic, yes?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he does. I suppose he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can Your Honour give me a minute? I think you better have this document -- it better go on the ELMO. I'm afraid we've put a circle around the word and I'm confused. I'd like to -- I would be assisted by name from the defence if they are saying that this is the only signed version of a Croatian version of this summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we can see on the ELMO, if you'd like to look at it, please, Mr. Marusic, what we can see on the ELMO in the Croatian version is that in paragraph six, you make reference to the head of the municipality Niko Grubesic. In the English version that we've been supplied, the municipality leader is Zoran Maric. Can you explain that from wherever the offices were that this document was prepared? Can you explain how it could be that what's set out there, apparently, as Niko Grubesic is completely transposed as Zoran Maric? Was there any mention of Zoran Maric by you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I did not mention Mr. Zoran Maric within this context. I mentioned Zoran Maric within the context of these ranks. That is, that Niko Grubesic and Zoran Maric also had those reserve ranks, so perhaps this is how this error was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you also explain how it is that in your summary you make no reference at all to the discussion that you claim to have had with Gavro Maric? Because it's not there in the document at all.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, he comes from that other establishment, that is, from the defence administration in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you spoke about --

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Not mentioned by name. That is, I felt it was not necessary to mention certain names. But because this happened in the office of the head, that is how I mention it. I could have also omitted this name. It could have been the then-head of the municipality and said just that, because I presume it is common knowledge who was the head of the municipality at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness have Exhibit 1477.6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before you made this detailed recommendation, Mr. Marusic, you had to know the type of awards that could be made, didn't you? Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you obtain the information as to what type of award could be made, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: At a meeting of the Travnik Defence Administration. That is, the Travnik Defence Administration was made of ten offices, and eight awards were envisaged for it. And one could nominate people for decorations from the lowest to the highest, except there was a recommendation. But decorations are not restricted to one office. One could nominate anyone who had sufficient merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You needed to know the criteria for any particular proposed decoration, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, there were certain criteria; that is, there was, well, service during a period of time. And we complied with criteria which at that time, in the organisation of the defence, and that is people who made a significant contribution, so as to have those people in the early days of the service, when we had it worst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the usher is standing and waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. I prepared him too early. If I can just ask a couple more questions. I don't want to trouble the usher, but if he can stand there for a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, you must have had written criteria; correct? You can't just do it on guesswork. You must have had written criteria.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Travnik Defence Administration received the criteria from the Ministry of Defence of the then-Herceg-Bosna, so the criteria which had to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at them, and if you'd like to have the original -- do you speak English, in fact?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd like to have the original, and if the usher would be good enough, please, to lay the first English sheet, which begins Article 1 and 2, on the ELMO. Now, what you were dealing with, you must have appreciated, was military decorations intended for members of the Croatian army. You appreciated that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time there was one set of rules, at the time, that is, after the war, when all the military institutions were nominating for decorations. So that those members of the office who had made -- announced any contribution, because the war lasted until the end of 1995 and the army was still engaged. Those people who stayed in the formations and also the members of the office who had made an outstanding contribution --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The answer to my question is yes, you appreciated you were dealing with military decorations for members of the Croatian army; yes?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: This is the instruction about military decorations. There are no other instructions. But we also requested that employees of our own institutions and of civilian institutions also be awarded for their merits. Now, the problem -- yes, of course the difficulty is true, that we had this tentative act about decorations, and now it had to be reworded and use the terminology for us who were the civilian part of the Ministry of Defence. And we were trying, at all costs, that we, as a civilian institution, also be awarded certain decorations for our merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course you must be allowed to answer at length if it's truly helpful, but you've used the words "tentative act." Are you saying that some other document, some proposal in written form that we all ought to be looking at, to explain what it is you were doing in making this recommendation? Or do you accept that you were making a proposal to Croatia for a military decoration, as I've just suggested? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a proposal. I've just -- I don't really know how you understood me. We reworded this military decoration. That is, we tried to take this, to send it for employees, because we were employees of the Ministry of Defence, but we were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please look at the second entry on this first page. It says: "The Grand Order of Petar Kresimir IV with Sash and Morning Star." And if we look, or if the Judges remember, what you were proposing was a decoration of the order of King Petar Kresimir IV with Sash and Morning Star. If the usher would be good enough to move to the second page of the exhibit on the ELMO, and if you would like to turn to the second page of the original, what we find is this, in the law on decorations and Honours in the Republic of Croatia. In the middle of the page it says this, in bold letters: "The president of the Republic of Croatia confers decorations on the basis of a legal document entitled 'The Decision on the Conferral of Decorations' on his own initiative or that of the State Commission for Decorations and Honours. The Commission for Decorations and honours is part of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. After processing incoming nominations, it submits them to the State Commission for Decorations and Honours. The Commission members are officers of the Croatian army who make their decisions on the basis of standards of consistency, exclusively at sessions of the Commission." Now, you were making an application for an award in line with these regulations, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, while we were deliberating the proposal, the nomination that we should make for Mr. Kordic, we tried -- because it was of a very local nature, we wanted to have a man who would become a bearer of a high decoration, because everybody thought him an honest and honourable man and we thought that it would be good for us to have in our midst a man --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am going to stop you. If what you're saying is suitable for further examination, Mr. Kordic's counsel can deal with it. Will you please answer my question. You were making an application for an award in line with, in accordance with, these regulations. Now, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, in a manner of speaking; that is, we, in a way -- this was merely a basis for us to propose -- it was difficult to reword it for our institution. We wanted to get decorations. We wanted people to be awarded. But we did not have it -- we did not have the instruction for that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But who were you applying to for an award if not to Croatia? Can we see it on the form? Were you applying to Mr. Boban for an award or the mayor of the municipality? Who were you applying to? You were applying to Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, we were in charge of sending this proposal to the defence administration of Travnik, and then further on there were these other levels through the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So you don't know where it was going.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, all decorations -- well, I think they were supposed to go to the Republic of Croatia, but at that time, in then-Herceg-Bosna, we did not have any decorations of our own, so that is what was used. I mean, these rules, that's what was asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next sheet in the English. Make sure it's the right one. And you can turn, please, to the next sheet in your version. And this is Article 8, which is the criteria for this award. It says this: "The Grand Order of ..." And then, first of all, it's Queen Jelena, "... and the Grand Order of Petar Kresimir IV with Sash and Morning Star, is conferred upon: dignitaries, high-ranking state officials, and heads of international organisations for their contributions to the international prestige and position of the Republic of Croatia." That is not the grounds for which you sought an award for Mr. Kordic, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No. These were not grounds for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Item 2. Croatian and foreign speakers of parliament and prime ministers for exceptional contributions to the independence and integrity of the -- next page -- Republic of Croatia, the establishment and advancement of the Republic of Croatia, and extraordinary contributions to the fostering of relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian people in other states." That was not the criteria upon which you were seeking this award for Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Which article is this? I haven't followed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies, Article 8 paragraph 2, perhaps you'd like to read it to yourself and then answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it please be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: How could I answer this? We tried when proposing this to have as many decorations as possible. At that time, we did not interpret these rules that much. We were just looking at which decorations there were and which decorations we could get and as many as possible and as high level as possible. We did not really go into all of this. We were told that these rules applied to military personnel and that we somehow had to fit into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third category is the only one that you relied on and I'll just read it, and then we'll look at your recommendations. "The highest-ranking military officials of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia for outstanding contributions in developing military strategy and doctrine, for merit in building up the Croatian army and for extraordinary successes in commanding and controlling armed forces units of the Republic of Croatia." It then says, "The grand order is conferred upon the highest-ranking military officials." And that, "Only two orders have been awarded to date." Now that was the category into which you were putting Mr. Kordic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you we did not really look at how many people had received these decorations. We did not look at the rules that much. We tried to propose as many decorations as possible. We wanted to have a man from our own environment with the highest possible decoration. We were guided by those words that, at the beginning, when these units were being established -- I mean these persons who were not being sent to do their military service, this remained among the people in Busovaca and beyond as the greatest thing. Somebody had to face this army so when we were making these proposals, we were guided by these facts more than we were guided by these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to have another look, very briefly, at the document that we were looking at before, if that could be laid on the ELMO. It's 1477 in the English and I'd like the witness, of course, to have the Croatian version to look at. It's the part 4 recommended text. You've told the Judges and I'm just going to have to summarise it that this was all to do with civilians and indeed you emphasised it by saying it was the speeches he made and the things he said simply to civilians. Now, if we look at the text that you wrote with such care, it starts off in this way: "As chief of the Busovaca defence office at the very start of the aggression against the Republic of Croatia, he organised and started all activities aimed at blocking the Serbo-Chetnik military in Central Bosnia." Well that relates to the early part of the conflict, doesn't it? Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next sentence, "For his outstanding contribution to the formation of Croatian Defence Council units." HVO units means military units, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "The creation of war strategy." What is war strategy if it isn't a military activity?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I -- I told you earlier that when I came to this office, I had just completed my university studies that were technical. My task was to bring this all together in to some kind of an entity so that this text would carry certain weight, and in addition to all of that, I had to choose all these words. Strategy, doctrine; I've been through a war, but until the present day, I don't know what these words really mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were building on the information and intelligence given you by other people to whom you spoke; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I personally knew -- I just asked other people about who worked in this office from 1991 until 1994. Over 20 persons had gone through that office in that period of time, there were four or five heads of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you can answer the question. You were building on the information and intelligence given you by other people to whom you spoke; is that not what your very evidence has been, please? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No. I personally knew about Mr. Kordic's efforts at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell us, please, what does "war strategy" mean? Just explain it to the Judges what you meant when you wrote "war strategy".

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: For me, then, it meant, well, we were outnumbered and these words that could be heard from Mr. Kordic. I mean, although we were outnumbered, although we had less soldiers, if we were entrenched in this area, that our people at home would be safe and we would be there at the front line entrenched on the ground so that if the enemy were to defeat us, the enemy had to cross our lines, the enemy would actually have to get to our trenches in order to chase us out of there. That is how I understood all of this. So every day I was digging away and other people were already making fun of me because of all this digging. But that's what it meant for me. At the beginning of the conflict, people didn't realise what this war was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have to move on. Let's look at the last -- the next sentence of this first paragraph. This is what you said, "And for his great success in leading and commanding the Croatian Defence Council units," which we know are military units, "during the Muslim aggression in the Lasva Valley and the wider region." The Muslim aggression in the Lasva Valley relates to 1993, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not to any earlier period?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, can you please tell us, and perhaps the witness should have his summary, I don't mind in which version, can you explain to us why, in paragraph nine of your summary, please -- have you got the version before you that you were looking at? Perhaps you can have it. Have you got your summary before you? It was there. There it is. Paragraph nine. You say this, "Mr. Kordic was not a military person. In spite of him not being in the military, he did play an important role during the first period of organising and creating the HVO formations in the area. He also played a prominent part in the blockade of several JNA arms of convoys that were passing through the territory of Busovaca at the end of 1991 and 1992. We were aware that Mr. Kordic had neither led nor commanded HVO forces in Busovaca. I know this from my personal experience because I was a soldier." Now your summary seeks, does it not, to justify the grant of this award entirely on the basis of what Mr. Kordic did in 1991 and 1992? I'm correct on that, aren't I?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I explained this. For example, when the Croats of Travnik were expelled together with their families and earlier on when they came from Jajce, when they were expelled by the JNA, by the Serb army, many of these expelled soldiers and civilians came to Busovaca. This guidance that was given to people to stay there in that area, also these people from Zenica too, that was important for me because everybody had wanted to leave. That was important for me. People were given this guidance to stay on when things were the most difficult for them, when they remained without anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, you've got an important job and you are an educated man. Please try and follow the question. Your summary seeks to justify the grant of this award entirely upon the basis of what Mr. Kordic did in 1991 and 1992 and you will remember, I asked you, when I related it to the question His Honour Judge Bennouna asked you whether the summary was complete, whether you'd been caused to think of anything else by being taken through the recommendations and so on and you said the summary was complete. The summary seeks to justify the award on the basis of 1991 and 1992 and no further. Am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I said that we had two critical periods there. One with the JNA army, and the other one was the conflict, the aggression of the Muslim army and this period was also important. It was important to have people remain in that area. As I said, every day, people were getting killed. Less and less people wished to stay so this moral leadership that we got from Mr. Kordic in terms of staying on, this meant giving guidance to civilians and the military, but this was only moral support and moral guidance. It meant a great deal to us in the army and to civilians, every address of that kind. But all our orders were received from the military, so this was not as if he were a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to just come back to the sentence on the recommendation and just draw to your attention also paragraph 10 above which, perhaps, the usher would be good to move just so that we can see 10 right the way down to 15. Ten says, "Period for which the decoration is proposed, 1991 to 1994." And the sentence that I've just read you which leads into the sentence that His Honour Judge Bennouna asked you about, is this: "For his great success in leading and commanding the Croatian Defence Council units during the Muslim aggression against the Lasva Valley and the wider region. During the bloodiest moments of the ordeal of the Croats in Central Bosnia, he played a key role in the battles and was a source of hope and faith in their survival," and so on. On the basis of intelligence coming to you, Mr. Marusic, even if you weren't there yourself, you were recording the fact that Kordic had acted as a military leader and it is as simple as that; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I already told you. Before, in order to fit into this law on decorations, we had to use some words. This had to be reworded. It was not that he was a leader of the military as an outstanding politician. He had these messages for civilians when things were most difficult for the people of Zenica, when they were coming all of them and when they all wanted to leave, he talked to them, he provided them with accommodation in the territory of Busovaca, he gave them places to stay. They were not staying in big sports halls or something, they were staying with friends or relatives. So that left a very favourable impression upon all these people who were left without a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marusic, the functions you have just described to us, can they there be exercised by Mr. Kordic without him being in any kind of relationships with the military? Do you mean to say that all these various functions of resistance, because it is tantamount to that, isn't it, that's what you're saying to us, whatever forms it may have taken in a critical period, can all these functions be exercised without there being a permanent and direct relationship with whose trade it is to carry out battles; in other words, with the military?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, for sure he had contacts in that period, but all these other military orders were issued by military personnel. It would be ridiculous if he functioned apart from everyone else. He had cooperation with everyone else, and they probably agreed on what kind of messages he was supposed to convey. And he conveyed messages to civilians which left quite an impact on all of us, including us in the military, but we received our orders in the military. So, yes, there must have been some kind of connection because nobody was acting just on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marusic, could this be qualified as a coordinating function, function as a coordinator?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know all these roles. I don't know which words should be used for this, but he functioned as a politician. I mean, he saw what the situation was on the ground, and he addressed the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. The Tribunal is interested in your own perspective and your own perception as a witness. Did you perceive him to be a leader, a leader?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: During wartime, I had practically never seen Mr. Kordic live. I only heard messages. I saw him as a moral leader, a moral leader. I mean, how we could stay on the front line. I already said that I was digging all the time, because we were supposed to be entrenched there. That meant a turning point for me. At the beginning of the war, we were not entrenched in the field at all and we had lots of casualties, but this was this turning point for us and for the military and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. You mentioned this digging on several occasions, and with respect, it doesn't help us. What I want to ask you is this: When you sent this form in, you were trying to be honest, I take it. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I tried, and there was a recommendation as far as this writing was concerned, to give words of praise and that all of this had to be put into a framework that would mean being an entity, and also to give words of praise. This is what would be read if a person were to be actually given a decoration. I tried to choose all these words and that finally if this person were to give -- to be given a decoration, I wouldn't want anyone to laugh when this would be read out, why this person got a decoration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You wouldn't want to mislead either those responsible for awarding the decoration or the general public, would you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I would not. I would not. I mean, simply among the people, there was such high regard for Dario. His messages were such that in the case of these words that I chose then, they would simply accept them. Nobody would be misled. Because especially people like I, at the time, and now also, these words -- some of these words -- well, we did not interpret them that way, the way this Court does, in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us with this: Why did you not simply say that he was an inspiring leader who made speeches to the population and kept their morale up in difficult times? Why not, if that were the truth, why did you not say it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a short explanation, but this text was supposed to have a certain length and also to consist of certain words. Such a high decoration cannot be explained somehow only with one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's now nearly 11.00. Are you going to be very much longer, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was coming rapidly to the end of all I wanted to ask him, but we were only expecting this witness on Thursday or Friday and I've got, I gather, something to consider about his testimony, which I can deal with over the break. So if I could just have an opportunity to round off after the break, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll adjourn. I understand that there's no other witness here. Is that right, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Gerritsen didn't come in until about 5.00, 5.30 last night, and he's still looking over his statement, or his outline, and making amendments to it, and we expect to have him here tomorrow. Actually, he's not scheduled to be back in our office until 3.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll lose some time, but we are not sitting beyond the lunch adjournment today in any event. You can conclude him tomorrow, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, it may be convenient, in the time that we have available, to deal with the affidavits. I notice there are five outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are prepared for that and we've got our usual schedule ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Marusic, we're going to adjourn for half an hour. During the adjournment, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, don't let anybody speak to you about it, and that does include members of the Defence team. Be back at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic, a change of topic just briefly. Are you still the head of the Busovaca Police Station?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, before you completely change the subject, I should like to ask a question about the document which is still on the ELMO, and I should like to ask a question of Mr. Marusic. That is: Witness, was Mr. Kordic aware of the content of this proposal or did he know of the proposal itself, that he was being nominated for a decoration?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I do not think he knew about the content, as far as I know; the content, the subject of the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that he knew about the proposal?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Possibly later on, since every information spreads around, he may have learned of the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this text wasn't shown him previously?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To follow on His Honour's question, before I turn to the other topic: At the time that this recommendation was made, Kordic was already indicted to come to this Tribunal, wasn't he, and Busovaca must have known about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly at that time the date of the indictment and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying you, as a Busovaca resident and, at that time, head of the defence office, weren't aware that the man for whom you were making this recommendation was actually already charged with war crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, not quite. I wasn't quite aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a teeny bit aware, were you?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Why, no. Bosniak media, the Muslim ones, wrote about that, as if they were guilty. That is how I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, once indicted, is the position this, that Mr. Kordic wasn't in Busovaca but was being protected in Croatia, to your knowledge? Is that the reality?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I used to see Mr. Kordic in Mostar during my studies there, and I don't really know where he was at all times during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't see him, did you, in Busovaca, after the time when you made this recommendation and indeed, perhaps until the time when you saw him here in Court. Did you see him between those two times?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And may this be the position with which you can help us that although the local department, your office, made a recommendation for an award that reflected the reality of what Mr. Kordic had done, others judged it unwise to give him an award now that he had been indicted. Isn't that the reality of what happened?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I don't think that was it. That is, the text was approved, I suppose, only on the basis of duties one discharged. I suppose others knew exactly what duties he discharged and so perhaps it was the text itself which did not pass muster because there were several levels of decision making, and I suppose these awards were conferred upon other people for those roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's quite right, and the reference number is 1476.2, but I shan't take the Chamber to it, it's quite right that President Tudjman signed off on a large number of awards in respect of a large number of Bosnians for their role in the war and approved their awards; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I do remember some decorations that came to the office. I mean Bosnian, Croats from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I'm suggesting to you, you know perfectly well, perhaps, that it was wiser heads in Croatia that decided it would be imprudent to go through with this award for Mr. Kordic once he was indicted if he never got the award. Do you think that's possible?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I do not think this proposal ever left the Travnik defence administration, or perhaps the military district of the time. That is more likely because had Mr. Kordic had any military role, somebody from the army must have -- would have proposed him, because it was the army people who were nominating their members for -- their people for awards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You come here with neither a piece of paper or a letter that deals with what I think you described as the instructions that civilians should be given awards, and you have no letter explaining how it was, if it be the case, that this particular recommendation wasn't taken further, do you? You don't have, as it were, a letter, you don't produce a letter at the start of or at the end of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. The instruction was only for employees, because we asked for it to take an initiative to award employees who worked in that institution so that is what we had. This instruction which the administration, the defence administration of the civilian sector in Central Bosnia, and we were to -- we were to be allotted eight decorations for employees who were the civilian part of the administration in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are a friend of Josip Grubesic's, aren't you, Kordic's bodyguard?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Not a friend. He works for the police administration. I mean, I did not even know him until I came to the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the two of you got into some difficulties with international police force recently, didn't you, operating together in relation to some document matter, but you got into difficulties together, IPTF, yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No, they were not difficulties, but we, in police administration, have advisors from the international police. And there was a case, if that is it, the case because a female employee was dismissed by the decision of the management board because the new president of that cooperative asked for the intervention of the police because that particular female employee, the secretary, had taken away all the documentation, all the money. So that there was a conflict there, and we were called in, that is, the police were called in, and then Niko Grubesic and other policemen went to see what it was all about, in order to verify the allegations. And the advisor who looked at the complaint of the respondent here says that we had done wrong and he wrote an application, he wrote a report. But it was rejected both by the headquarters of our IPTF in Sarajevo and by our -- so it was the mistake of that advisor. He only received information of one party without any proof from the other side and I -- from the -- IPTF commissar, I received a reply that this report was being rejected and that I had done right, because that was not the case for the police and then private charges were filed against that lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to deal with these matters in detail. Are you still head of the police office, the police station?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just back to the document then, because there are only a couple more questions I needed to ask you, if we look at it, perhaps the usher, if I could prevail on him, could move it up so that the ELMO -- just a little bit on this occasion, just to understand so we can see the first box. He's described as a brigadier because he was a brigadier, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the general form and what to fill in the particulars from the personal card and he was awarded this rank of a brigadier like other politicians. As I told you, these are his personal data.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Like which politicians, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, all those politicians at that time, those who discharged various duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I mean politicians from Busovaca, I don't know about others. I know about Busovaca politicians, Zoran Maric, Niko Grubesic, so they were the ones, those in Busovaca, and there are others who have those ranks even if lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All brigadiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No, lower ranks. I think Zoran Maric was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Grubesic, what rank was he given?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: I think that of a captain, I'm not sure, but I do know that he has a rank, and I think he is a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will be corrected if I'm wrong, of course, I think Mr. Maric may have told us that he was a civilian throughout. Are you saying he had and used a rank or are you just making it up? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, a civilian, but he was -- I mean those politicians and civilians who played important parts, so this was the rank of reserve officers, was granted to them, that is, those civilians and politicians who had some merits, and he is a politician, and Zoran was a politician then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Staying with the document just a couple more boxes, for to you explain to us since you filled it in. To the right of brigadier, "Branch Military Occupational Speciality", what you wrote down was "PJS/OVS", and the expansion of that is not known to the translator so the original simply says PJS/OVS. What does it mean, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: This is the service of the army, so this is infantry general, the simplest specialities depending on the service of the branch of the army. That means that he was trained for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It also -- does it not fit, infantry, with what you wrote in the box "Commanding Croatian Defence Council units." Doesn't it fit?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No. I told you, I mean, he had -- in the former JNA, he served in the infantry and it was under that, he had no rank. But amongst the proposals, I suppose, and when proposals were sent, one wrote in what branch of the army one served with the former JNA and it was for that particular branch, I mean. So that was how the proposal was written for the rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Marusic --

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: -- regarding the branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at boxes 10 and 11, although there is a slight inconsistency between the two in that one of them speaks of 1991, look at box 11. The 8th of April, 1992, why did you choose that date?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Quite simply I had it on the -- in the books, and I saw that he was -- that he moved on when others -- when other people took up, assumed those duties that that was the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your answer. Can you explain to me, please, why you chose the date the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, because according to the books, according to the records, another person assumed that duty, head of the office, and he moved to another -- I mean, that is, another person began to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which office?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: That is what I knew at the time. The office, the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992, just to remind you, if you need it, the presidency of the HZ HB established the HVO. Would you like to think again, please, why you chose the date the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I've said it. According to the office records, another person began to discharge that duty, and he moved away. That is, he left that office simply, that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a one-word answer will do to this. Are you really telling the Judges that that date has absolutely nothing to do with the establishment of the HVO and it's all a coincidence? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, to me, it was just a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not telling this Chamber the truth, and I'm going to suggest to you that when you drew and signed -- when you drafted and signed your summary seeking to justify this award all on the basis of what happened in 1991 and 1992, you were knowingly not telling them the truth either. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I here read this oath, that I would speak the truth, and to the best of my recollection, it was as I have told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A great deal was said about this proposal which is before you, Mr. Marusic. Only a few brief questions. Did you ever talk with Mr. Dario Kordic before you wrote and signed this proposal?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you, before you wrote this proposal, talk to any military person in Busovaca, such as Dusko Grubesic, Jure Cavara, or perhaps any other military from the Operative Zone, that is, subsequent military district of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Today you repeatedly said -- even when asked by Their Honours, you explained that you were trying to reword and fit your proposal into that legal text, that is, the instructions that you had been given. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was difficult for this to be acceptable. It had to be properly fashioned. It had to be properly done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You already gave us your opinion about this. And that proposal, if I understood you well, did not pass muster at high levels, so either at the Travnik defence administration or the Ministry of Defence of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna; is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it was at the level of the military district where the administration's proposal was to go. I mean, the command, where the army was, perhaps at that level. But they perhaps stopped that because he knew that he had not discharged the duties and that other people had been awarded for those duties as army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Does that mean that you failed to properly fit your proposal, to use your words, into the criteria laid down?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What we wanted did not come true. I think that perhaps this text should have had a different content. Because it was presented here that it was for these merits, for the doctrine and strategy, but it was military officials who were awarded for those merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A few times you stressed this, but the core of the matter, if you agree, is that the defence office consisted of civilians and that they carried out civilian duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Civilians, civilian duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And precisely because they carried out civilian duties and they were engaged throughout the war, they did not have any other possibility of getting decorated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The document that we introduced at the end, that is, D283/1, it shows that this proposal was never accepted at higher levels, which shows how well justified your claim is that at a level higher than yours, this proposal was halted because it did not meet the criteria.

utterances.speaker: IVO MARUSIC
utterances.text: Precisely. It was halted because it was decided at lower levels that this proposal should not go any further up, and obviously somebody else got this decoration. There were proposals that were sent for other men who were members of the military, which means that it is not true that somebody from Croatia decided that it should not be given, possibly because of the proceedings that were brought against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Marusic. Your Honours, I do wish to apologise to the Court and to the Prosecutors for the mistake in the translation that was due to technical reasons purely. Mr. Marusic worked on the Croat original version of his document and then there was this mistake in the transcript. So we do apologise once again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Marusic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with the affidavits, the five which we have: a Mr. Jure Pelivan, Perica Juric, Josip Goludza, Stanislav Nussbaum, and Anto Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour has our schedule, I trust. I'm sorry if it hasn't been -- it can be dealt with singly, of course, in the way that the Court prefers. The Court may -- and of course the Court will remember our general position of opposition, subject to the approach we take. But the Court will see that the first one, we invite the Court to say, should not be given by affidavit. As to the second one, subject to a particular point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's look at them point one by one, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The first one, the comment on the right-hand column really says it all. This is an affidavit so broad, covering areas frequently without the basis of assertions and it's difficult to find specific points in the live evidence which it corroborates. A lot of it seems to be hearsay and general opinion. If you look at what it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to say, is there any particular matter which you would wish to draw our attention to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. But if Your Honour looks at the very title of the witness, on item 1, and then reminds yourself of the breadth and generality of his evidence, the Court may decide it simply isn't evidence that should come in by affidavit because it can't really help. There are always problems of assessing affidavit evidence in any event, but on a general account like this, it's really hard to see how it fits the Rules for affidavit, which the Defence say have to be applied strictly, or how can it assist in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We think this affidavit is broadly corroborative of evidence which we've heard, and applying the Rules, which we have done, we can see no reason not to admit it. So it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one, we raise no special points, subject to what we observe at point 4. There's a suggestion that there's an incorporation of an important bit of law, if it ever were incorporated, but which -- we're unable to understand the alleged Geneva Convention on human rights.
