I don't know what at all is being referred to there. No doubt it will be relied on as important by the Defence in due course, but we can't conceivably understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The only point that was raised, I think, by the Prosecution is the document that was adopted by the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Your Honour. It was actually signed by Perica Juric. It's already been exhibited as document 183/1, tab 9, and it's basically a document dated September 30th, 1993, titled "A Declaration on the Adoption of Documents on the Protection and Exercise of Human Freedoms and Rights." And I'm sure the Court will have in mind that the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan actually contained a list of the international human rights instruments which were to be incorporated by any republics that were to be formed pursuant to that plan, and this document adopts that in haec verba and in exactly the same order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one, Goludza, would seek to give evidence of representing the RBiH in economic and trade matters, of the functioning of the office in Zagreb as an office in exile, as a split of aid, and all these matters, as we understand it, could have been covered with live evidence, but have only been raised in the affidavit of Pelivan so this would be, as it were, a corroboration of affidavit by affidavit which is plainly not envisaged and cannot be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My recollection of the evidence, Your Honour, is that Witness DJ and Zoran Perkovic both gave evidence about the establishment of an agency of the -- an office of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb intended to insist in humanitarian aid matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to reply on that, maybe in short form, yes, but none of the detail, so this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It sounds as though it's a matter of record rather than anything else. Is it really a controversial matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may or may not be controversial, probably isn't particularly controversial, but whether it's going to assist the Chamber by adding more paper in the form of affidavits which is going to be difficult to evaluate for their truth value when there is nothing of a like kind that they support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this may be of marginal significance. It's certainly, as far as we can see, not a controversial matter, his evidence, except perhaps what he says about Mr. Kordic but, nonetheless, that's not a matter which he needs to be cross-examined on and, in fact, it hasn't been suggested that he would be. And in those circumstances, we propose to admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I quite understand. We ought perhaps to make it clear, and I'm grateful to Ms. Somers for reminding me that we, of course, don't accept the particular terminology position "government in exile" or anything like that. Stanislav Nussbaum comes next, this is the personnel commission, a decision signed by Jadranko Prlic never holding meetings. What's being set out here on the right-hand column, there's an excerpt from the LiveNote of Buntic which is perhaps helpful in showing how limited is the material that is now sought to support by this affidavit evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I remember him saying that the commission never met, I made a particular note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you look at what he actually said, starting at the top of the page, I suppose one could explain it for a long time, perhaps, their Presidency and government often debated why this person was appointed, why not that one, why two individuals. So perhaps it occurred to somebody that a personnel commission could be set up, then ought to take care of an equitable number of heads of deputies or whatever. I suppose that that was the purpose. Then in the last answer, I don't really think I can help you because it would probably require regulations. He plainly knew very little about it and if we're now going to have a detailed affidavit trying to explain the position for founding something for the Defence argument, there are serious problems in the evidential position that will confront the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To respond very briefly to that, Mr. President, the Court can look at this affidavit for itself and determine whether it's very detailed or not. Basically Mr. Nussbaum says: These were the members of the commission. The commission never met from the time that the document was signed by Dr. Prlic to the time I left for Rijeka and, to the best of my knowledge, this commission took absolutely no action. And that Mr. Kordic obviously took no role within the committee, that was essentially nonexistent. So I don't see how that can possibly be described as detailed and it certainly is completely corroborative of the very clear testimony that Mr. Buntic gave on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's not clear to me what you are seeking, cross-examination or the exclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The court will remember that our attitude on affidavits is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour will recall our attitude is formal objection to all affidavits because they all raise matters that are in issue. I think there may be one affidavit where we've specifically said that nothing is at issue but only one, but consistent with the Chamber's ruling where the Chamber's considering affidavits, we then distinguish between those where they draw your attention to particular matters which might merit particular argument and where we don't. So far as this witness is considered, we are not pressing you against admitting it but we are drawing to your attention for the exercise of your discretion the limited nature of detail in the evidence already available and to contrast it with the affidavit that would be forthcoming. We aren't, ourselves, particularly concerned. We don't press the point on this affidavit, but that's not the end of the matter because it's the discretion of the Trial Chamber and not of us. And self-evidently, on one hand, we would rather everything goes in by affidavit because it shortens the trial on the other hand. We'd self-evidently like to cross-examine everything that's in issue. But essentially we are taking a neutral position simply letting the Chamber decide for itself once we've drawn to your attention points that may help you in the exercise of your discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit this one. The final one is (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is one again where we don't raise any specific objections but the Chamber might, with this witness, just like to have in mind that the witness confirmed -- the witness being supported, Jure Cavara, because we suspect he's quite strong in one's memory from last week, and giving answers, I can forecast, if we deal with these things in detail in closing briefs, will be subject to the comments of the complete improbability of much of what he was saying. Now, it's true that the corroborative material goes to a few topics and we can see them listed on the right-hand side that the first topic he deals with would appear to corroborate as with the second about the date and as with, of course, number five which is a common theme. But it may be with this, just as an example, the Chamber's got to give some consideration to the particular live witness because, of course, if with this witness, as indeed with all of them, if the witness is himself utterly rejected as incredible or beyond acceptable limits of credibility, why then is nothing that the affidavit will ever corroborate. That's a general point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit this. That deals with the affidavits. The other matter I wanted to raise was the issue of timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And really I think it's Mr. Mikulicic who I would be grateful if we could hear from first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not wish to repeat what my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, said the other day concerning the problems encountered by Mr. Cerkez's Defence. However, by way of illustration, I can say that we are in a position now to be looking at some 800 documents that had just appeared before us during these past few days. They are directly related to military matters in the crucial period for Vitez and the area of Novi Travnik. However, I'm saying this so that you would understand the kind of problems that we are facing. Nevertheless, in spite of this, we can confirm with certainty that we shall present our evidence, our case, within six to eight weeks. So if we were to start presenting our case as was recently mentioned, on the 24th of July, then we would have two weeks prior to the summer break, and after that, six weeks at the most, in the autumn. Therefore, I can confirm with certainty, I believe, that Mr. Cerkez's Defence would conclude its case by the 20th of October, as you had said yesterday that that was your plan. However, in this respect, I do wish to say that I kindly ask for some flexibility in terms of the presentation of our case. It may happen that some witnesses may appear all of a sudden. We gave a list which was based on the knowledge we had then. However, there may be some changes which, at any rate, will not be of major significance. Therefore, I can confirm that by the date you mentioned yesterday, we will certainly have completed our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I thank you. Two matters, really. The first is that at some stage we must schedule a pre-defence conference for Mr. Cerkez's case. We'll have to fix a date during the next two weeks or so, I would anticipate. So perhaps you might like to have that in mind. The second matter is the dates you've given. In fact, I now find that the 20th, by the 20th of October, you will have actually had seven weeks in the autumn, if my mathematics is right. That would give you a total of nine weeks. Do you think you might finish more quickly or can't you say at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, at this point in time I could not commit myself. However, there is a high degree of probability that we might finish sooner, one week sooner at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards your suggestion concerning the date for a pre-defence conference, I am available and we shall certainly do our best to meet your request in this respect; that is to say, we expect you to set a date and we shall certainly comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, unless there's anything else you'd like to raise, Mr. Mikulicic, while you're -- perhaps while you're on your feet, the other point I wanted to raise with you was the question of rebuttal and rejoinder. Again, that may be primarily a matter for the Prosecution. Perhaps I better turn to Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I follow what Your Honour said yesterday, the plan is that rebuttal should start on the 4th of December and last with rejoinder for a maximum of two weeks. Just dealing with that as a proposition, that would mean that if the expectation is that closing briefs and closing argument is to be presented by Christmas, we are on a very tight timetable if not an impossible one, because that only leaves, after the end of the second week, I should think at the most two or three working days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean the suggestion is that -- the suggestion is the -- the proposal is that two weeks for all the concluding matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that would be any evidence, and any submissions. Post-trial briefs, whatever the term used is, or concluding briefs, would have to be prepared in the break before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course there's no problem with preparing closing briefs in the break and their being exchanged either ahead of the rebuttal case contingent on further evidence or indeed by amendment of almost concluded drafts the second or almost the second evidence concludes. So there's no particular problem there even though the requirement or necessity for say a minimum of a day for oral argument reduces still further the time available for rebuttal or rejoinder evidence. I simply cannot forecast what rebuttal evidence, if any, I shall seek to put in, but I think it's inevitable in light of two things, that there will be some. First, well-known, the production of documents elsewhere. Second, there have been several occasions throughout the case when really, by discussion and agreement, topics have been touched upon where the Court has said to us well, perhaps if that comes in at all, it will come in by rebuttal. And we've accepted that as a general indication and not pursued matters further. So there are some topics that I think are likely to be by rebuttal and my concern, as I've explained on several occasions, is that what's happening in Zagreb may, and I say "may" involve quite a lot of evidence. And I would inquire whether there is any chance of the 4th of December date being advanced by a week or so, particularly in light of what Mr. Mikulicic has said about the certainty that they will finish by the 20th of October and the possibility that they will finish earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The difficulty about that is the scheduling of the other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which may get more complicated and not easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll have these matters in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I should perhaps mention one other point that's occurred to us, and I should inform you of it. Depending on the decision of the Appeals Chamber in relation to affidavit evidence, and assuming that the decisions are before December, then it may be possible for some of our rebuttal case to be dealt with by affidavit. Alternatively, it may not. If there has to be strict compliance with a particular regime and we can't fit into that regime, why then we won't be able to offer material by affidavit. But alternatively, we may be able to do so. We have in mind that as our general preparation. But I would urge the Court to say, realistically, that it will be quite a squeeze to get everything in that last fortnight and to be away for Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might, Mr. President, just a couple of observations. We would greatly appreciate the courtesy of a little advanced notice with respect to the Prosecution's closing brief just so that we can respond in an appropriate way. I'm sure the Court knows that -- I can't see from the LiveNote right now, but I think we're up to about 22.000 pages in the trial transcript. There are thousands and thousands of exhibits. The summarisation obligations are going to be substantial in any event, and that, of course, will be compounded by any rebuttal evidence that has to be evaluated. I have not, frankly, given much thought to how we would propose to address that. Perhaps by way of a supplement to the brief, something like that. But I'm sure that the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or indeed orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Or orally, depending upon the magnitude of the case. Obviously, if we're talking about, you know, another thousand documents, I'm not sure that's really feasible to handle orally. But obviously, however the Court wants to do it, we'll do our best to comply. But I'm sure the Court doesn't need to be told from us, there are logistical problems that the lawyers face, and ultimately, of course, our job is to try to help the Trial Chamber with our view of the case. And it doesn't make any sense, to my mind, to work very hard on preparing a brief which has to be squeezed into the last minute and suffers in terms of completeness and flow as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that topic, if I could be heard for just a minute, there are really two issues there. As to exchange of closing briefs, I think the practice of this place, and the understandable practice, is mutual exchange followed by oral argument that can then deal with issues that need to be dealt with because they haven't been covered in closing briefs, and we would press most strongly that that is the entirely appropriate course. As to rebuttal evidence, of course I'll give every advance notice of rebuttal evidence that I can. I've already, I think, served one letter on the Defence indicating one witness who we may intend to call by way of rebuttal. And they can be quite confident that in accordance with my usually policy, as soon as I know what I'm intending to do in that area, I'll let them and the Court know for planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's mutual exchange rather than one responding to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think there's some merit in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will do all we can to provide other material in advance, and of course if at this stage of the trial it's possible to deal with more matters by way of agreement and admission, then we can save quite a lot of time, but we'd have to wait and see. The documents coming from Zagreb, as far as I know it, and from the way that were described by Mr. Kovacic, I think, last week, documents are being provided, in accordance with certain regimes, to all parties at the same time, or effectively at the same time, so that should, at least as to those documents that are being provided in that way, reduce the requirement for time to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's nothing else, we'll adjourn until tomorrow. We'll let you have the calendar as soon as we can. Perhaps the senior legal officer could have a word with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 12.36 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
